items.prompt: A trade association reports that Namibian households bought 6.2 million litres of long-life milk last year at an average price of N$18.00 a litre, and 6.5 million litres this year at an average price of N$19.50. Calculate the size of this market by value in each year, and the growth in its value.
items.canonical_answer:
Market size by value = units sold in the market x the average price paid.

Last year: 6.2 x 18 = 111.6, so N$111.6 million. This year: 6.5 x 19.5 = 126.75, so N$126.75 million.

Growth = (size at the end - size at the start) / size at the start. The increase is 126.75 - 111.6 = 15.15, and 15.15 / 111.6 = 0.136, so the market grew by 13.6% by value.

Volume grew by much less: 6.5 - 6.2 = 0.3 million litres, and 0.3 / 6.2 = 0.048, or 4.8%. Nearly nine tenths of the 13.6% came from the price rise rather than from more milk being sold, so a dairy planning extra bottling capacity on the value figure would be building for volume that is not there.
marking_guidance: Formula: market size by value = units sold x average price; growth = (end - start) / start.
Substitution must be shown, not only the answer.
Units: every figure carries N$ or litres; a percentage is labelled as a percentage.
Interpretation: one sentence saying what the gap between value growth and volume growth means for a producer's capacity decision.

items.prompt: A trade association reports that the market for ready-mixed concrete grew 15% by value last year while the volume sold fell by about 4%. Explain what those two figures mean for a batching plant deciding whether to buy a second mixer.
items.canonical_answer:
Compared with each other, the two figures say that the market is paying more for less: value can only have risen on a falling volume if the average price rose, and a 15% rise in value on a 4% fall in volume implies a price rise of about 20% per cubic metre.

What that means for the mixer is the point. A mixer adds capacity, and capacity is consumed by volume, not by value - and volume is what fell. Measured against last year, the plant is selling less concrete for more money, so this evidence does not support buying capacity; it supports protecting margin on the volume already being poured.

What the figures cannot say is why the price rose. If a competitor closed and the volume it served has not come back to the market, the picture may look different next year, so the figures set the decision for now rather than for good.
marking_guidance: Comparison: value growth must be read against volume growth, not on its own.
Meaning: the answer must say what the two figures together mean for the capacity decision.

items.prompt: Explain why a business needs to know the growth rate of its market and not only the growth in its own sales.
items.canonical_answer:
Its own sales figure cannot say where the extra sales came from. If sales rose 6% in a year when the market grew 15%, the business sold more and still lost ground, because it captured a smaller share of the expansion than its rivals did.

The reason the market figure is needed is that it separates sales the business won from sales the market handed it. Growth that came from the market expanding may stop as soon as the market stops expanding, and it says nothing about whether the offer is competitive. A business reading 6% on its own may treat a weakening position as a good year and leave it unattended until the market flattens.
marking_guidance: The reason must be given and developed, not only the fact restated.

items.prompt: In a market where three producers hold 45%, 30% and 15% of sales and the rest is spread among small yards, analyse the effect on a new entrant of the way that share is divided.
items.canonical_answer:
Starting point: 90% of the market is already committed to one of three established suppliers, so most sales the entrant makes have to be taken from a producer the buyer has already chosen.

Because those buyers have a supplier that already meets the need, they have little reason to move unless something changes for them, so the entrant has to offer either a lower price or a clear point of difference - faster delivery, or a grade the three do not carry. If it competes on price, the mechanism runs further: the established producers are larger, so they are likely to have lower costs per unit and can hold a matched price for longer than an entrant with no established volume.

The measurable consequence is a thinner contribution on the entrant's first sales and a longer period before it covers its fixed costs.

For the entrant's own objectives, that makes survival rather than share the binding constraint in the first year, which is why entry into a concentrated market is more often attempted on difference than on price.
marking_guidance: Condition: the concentrated share structure must be the stated starting point.
Mechanism: each step must explain why the next follows, not assert it.
Consequence: the chain must reach a measurable consequence for the entrant.
Objective: the answer must name the business objective the effect bears on.

items.prompt: A charcoal producer near Otjiwarongo is told that the regional market for packaged braai charcoal grew 18% by value last year while the tonnage sold across the market was unchanged, and that one producer holds 55% of it. Explain what those two facts together tell it about entering this market.
items.canonical_answer:
Take the two facts in turn and then together.

Value up 18% on unchanged tonnage means the whole of the growth came from price. Because no extra tonnage was sold, there is no new demand for a new producer to pick up: every tonne it sells has to come out of somebody else's tonnage.

One producer holding 55% tells it whose tonnage that is likely to be. A producer at that scale buys wood and packaging in larger quantities, so it is likely to have a lower cost per bag and can hold a reduced price longer than a new entrant with no established volume.

Put together, the conclusion is that this market looks attractive on the value figure and is not: entering it means taking tonnage from a larger, probably lower-cost rival in a market that is not growing in the quantity sold. If the producer enters at all, the case rests on a difference the leader does not offer - a pack size, a delivery window, a grade of charcoal - rather than on price.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must work from the two facts given: 18% value growth on flat tonnage, and a 55% share.
Reasoning: each fact must be linked by reasoning to what it means for a new entrant's sales.
Conclusion: the answer must conclude on whether and how to enter.

items.prompt: A new bakery in Katima Mulilo has profiled its first month of customers: most live within about two kilometres of the open market, buy five days a week, spend N$25 to N$40 a visit, and buy before eight in the morning on the way to work. It has N$8 000 to spend on either a delivery bicycle or an extra baker so it can open an hour earlier. Explain which of the two the profile supports.
items.canonical_answer:
Two facts in the profile settle it. Customers buy on a journey they already make, and they buy before eight.

Because they pass the shop on the way to work, delivery would be paying to solve a problem these customers do not have - the bread is already on their route. The same profile shows demand concentrated in a window the bakery cannot serve if it opens at eight, so every customer passing before then is a sale the shop is not in a position to make.

The conclusion is to spend the N$8 000 on the earlier opening. The answer would move if the profile showed customers spread through the day or living further out, because the binding constraint would then be distance rather than opening time.

items.prompt: Explain how building a customer profile out of characteristics a business can act on reduces wasted marketing spending.
items.canonical_answer:
A characteristic the business can act on is one that points at a decision it has to take anyway: where the buyers are points at the site and the delivery radius, what they can afford points at the price and the pack size, when they buy points at opening hours and at when to advertise.

Because each characteristic attaches to a decision, the spending follows the profile instead of being spread across a whole population: advertising is bought where those buyers are rather than town-wide, and stock is held in the sizes they buy. The waste that is removed is the money that would otherwise have reached people whose characteristics make them unlikely to buy.

A profile made of characteristics the business cannot act on - that customers are aged 25 to 45 and enjoy fresh bread - may be accurate and still changes no decision, so it removes no waste.
marking_guidance: The mechanism must be traced step by step, because an asserted effect is not an explained one.

items.prompt: A new juice bar in Ongwediva is deciding which flavours to launch. Explain the difference between primary and secondary research for this decision.
items.canonical_answer: The difference is who collected the data and for what purpose. items.prompt: Observation and test marketing are primary methods. Identify the evidence each one produces, and explain how that differs from what a questionnaire produces.
items.canonical_answer:
Observation produces a record of what people actually did - which shelf they stopped at, how long they queued, which route they took through the store. It captures behaviour but not the reason behind it, because nobody is asked.

Test marketing produces evidence of money changing hands: the product is sold for real in one town or one branch before a full launch, so what is measured is purchase rather than intention.

A questionnaire produces what people say - stated preferences, stated intentions and stated reasons - from many respondents at once, in a form that can be counted and scaled up. Its strength is coverage and its weakness is that a stated intention is not yet a purchase.
marking_guidance: Each method must be given the evidence it actually produces, and the contrast with the questionnaire must be stated rather than implied.
A two-part recall card: it asks about three methods at once, so it carries no single paper tariff.

items.prompt: Oshakati Poultry is deciding whether to sell packaged chicken portions. It holds its own till records showing which cuts sell in its butchery, a count its manager made of how many shoppers picked up packaged chicken in a rival's store, and a national report on meat consumption published last year. Explain which of these are primary and which are secondary, and which fits the decision least well.
items.canonical_answer:
The till records are secondary data even though they belong to the business: they were produced to record sales, not to answer this question. The manager's count is primary - the business gathered it itself, for this decision, however informal the method. The national report is secondary and external.

The reason the classification matters here is fit. The till records describe cuts sold loose to people who already shop at the butchery, so they say nothing about packaged portions or about shoppers who go elsewhere. The national report covers the country and not Oshakati, and a year-old figure for meat consumption does not separate packaged from loose.

So the till records fit the decision least well, because the one thing this decision turns on - whether people would buy the packaged form - is the one thing they cannot contain. The manager's count is the only evidence here that observes the actual behaviour in question.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must classify these three specific sources, not sources in general.
Reasoning: the reason each fits or does not fit must be linked to what the decision turns on.
Conclusion: the answer must conclude which source is weakest for this decision.

The shop's question suggests its own answer, so it collects agreement rather than information: asking 2 000 customers instead of 200 gathers more agreement, not better data. Because the results still come out as neat percentages, the bias is hard to see, which leads the shop to trust a figure that says little about whether customers actually find its prices reasonable.

items.prompt: A bakery's questionnaire asks its customers, 'Would you agree that our new rolls are good value at N$12?' Analyse how a question worded like that can lead the bakery to a decision that loses money.
items.canonical_answer:
Starting point: the question names the answer it wants, and it is being asked by the business itself, in its own shop.

Because agreeing is the easier and more polite response, and because disagreeing means telling the baker to his face that his rolls are overpriced, the proportion agreeing is pushed above the proportion who would actually pay N$12. The bakery reads the answer as a measure of willingness to pay when it is partly a measure of how the question was put.

It then bakes to the volume that figure implies and holds the price at N$12. The measurable consequence is unsold stock: rolls baked for demand that was never there, written off at the end of each day, and a price held too high to clear them.

The objective this bites is cash. A small bakery paying for flour before it sells bread can run short of working capital from a run of days like that long before the pricing error shows up in its annual figures.

items.prompt: A tailoring business in Gobabis has N$20 000 for research and is deciding whether to commission a primary study before launching a school-uniform line. Evaluate whether it should spend the money that way.
items.canonical_answer:
It should not commit the whole N$20 000 to fieldwork before it has looked at what already exists.

The decisive criterion is whether an existing source can answer the question at a fraction of the cost. Much of what this business needs to know is already recorded somewhere: how many learners attend the schools it would supply, which schools already have a contracted supplier, and what the current garments cost. Spending N$20 000 to discover figures obtainable for a few hundred is the most expensive way to learn them, and for a small tailoring business N$20 000 is capital that could buy a second machine.

The strongest argument the other way is real. The question the decision actually turns on - whether parents would switch supplier, and at what price - is not recorded anywhere, because the line does not exist yet. No desk research can settle that, and launching without it means committing fabric and machine time to a guess.

On balance the sensible course is to sequence the spending rather than choose between the two: establish from school rolls and existing prices whether the market is large enough to be worth entering, then spend what is left on a narrow primary study aimed only at the switching question. That way the fieldwork is bought for the part no other source can supply.

The judgement changes if the decision has to be made before a study could be run, or if the fabric commitment is small enough that a limited test run would cost less than the research.

Context: the answer must be argued for a small tailoring business with N$20 000, not for research in general.
Criterion: the decisive test is whether existing sources can answer part of the question more cheaply.
Counterargument: must acknowledge that the switching question cannot be answered from existing data.

items.prompt: Namib Fresh, a juice bottler in Oshakati, has four weeks and N$12 000 before it must choose between two bottle sizes. A research firm offers 150 in-store taste tests with a short questionnaire for N$11 000, delivered in three weeks. Explain whether this primary study is a good use of the money.
items.canonical_answer:
Three of Namib Fresh's own facts decide it: the question is a choice between two named options, the deadline is four weeks, and N$11 000 is almost the whole budget.

On fit, the study is well aimed. No published source records what Oshakati shoppers think of two bottle sizes that do not yet exist in this market, so this is a question only fieldwork can answer, and the firm's design puts the actual product in front of the actual shoppers. On timing, three weeks leaves a week to act, which fits. The weakness is the sample: 150 respondents carry a margin of about 8 percentage points, so a result of 52% against 48% would settle nothing, and the budget would be gone.

So it is a good use of the money on one condition - that Namib Fresh agrees in advance what gap between the two sizes it would treat as decisive, and what it does if the gap is smaller than that. Commissioned blind, it risks spending N$11 000 to learn that the two sizes are close, which is an answer the business could act on only by choosing on cost instead.

items.prompt: A guest house in Swakopmund is setting its 2027 prices using a national tourism report published in 2024 whose fieldwork was done in 2022, and which reports average spend for Namibia as a whole. Explain the two weaknesses in using it this way, and what would reduce them.

The second is coverage. The report averages Namibia as a whole, and Swakopmund is a coastal destination with its own season, its own visitor mix and its own competing supply. A national average blends it with lodges hundreds of kilometres away, so the figure the guest house would price against is not a figure about its own market.

Both are reduced the same way: by adding something current and local. The guest house's own booking records for the last two seasons give the recent local picture, and the published rates of nearby guest houses give the competitive one. The national report is then used for the direction of travel rather than for the level, which is the part it can support.

items.prompt: Analyse how a retailer that plans its product range from its own sales records alone can end up missing a growing part of its market.
items.canonical_answer:
Starting point: the sales records contain one population - the people who already buy from this retailer - and nothing about anyone else.

Because a product the retailer has never stocked generates no sales, it generates no record, so it appears in the data as absence of demand rather than as an untested question. The retailer reads the records, sees the lines that sell, and reorders those, which keeps the range where it is. The customers who wanted something else bought it elsewhere, and their purchase was recorded in a competitor's system.

The measurable consequence builds over time: the range narrows towards what the existing customers already buy, and sales growth slows towards the growth rate of that group, while a segment served by rivals expands outside the data.

For the retailer's objectives this shows up as a falling share of a growing market - sales that hold steady or drift up while the business's position weakens - which is exactly the pattern internal data is least able to reveal.

Consequence: the chain must reach a measurable consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why market research is normally carried out on a sample rather than on the whole target population.
items.canonical_answer:
Researching a whole population is rarely practical, for three connected reasons.

Populations are large: a bank asking every one of its 180 000 account holders would be running a national exercise rather than a piece of market research. Contacting all of them costs more and takes longer than the decision can justify, and the decision usually has a date by which it must be made, so a complete count can arrive after it is useless. And in many markets no complete list of the population exists to work from - there is no register of everyone who buys bread.

So the real choice is not between a sample and a complete count. It is between a sample and no evidence.

items.prompt: A retailer in Ondangwa surveys 400 of the 62 000 households in its catchment; 148 say they would buy a new product priced at N$25. Taking the margin of error as about 1 divided by the square root of the sample size, calculate the proportion saying yes, the number of households in the catchment that implies, and the range that the margin of error puts around it.
items.canonical_answer:
Proportion = respondents saying yes / sample size = 148 / 400 = 0.37, that is 37%.

Scaled to the catchment: 0.37 x 62 000 = 22 940 households.

Margin of error: the square root of 400 is 20, and 1 / 20 = 0.05, so about 5 percentage points either way. The true proportion is likely to lie between 32% and 42%, which is between 0.32 x 62 000 = 19 840 and 0.42 x 62 000 = 26 040 households.

The 22 940 is the middle of a range about 6 200 households wide, and the retailer's stock order has to be placed somewhere inside it: ordering for 22 940 treats a figure the survey did not establish as though it had.

Substitution must be shown, not only the answer.

items.prompt: Explain how a sample of shoppers approached at a shopping centre on two Saturday mornings can produce a misleading estimate of demand across a whole town.
items.canonical_answer:
Three filters act on the sample before a single question is asked. Everyone in it was at a shopping centre, everyone was there on a weekend morning, and everyone was willing to stop and answer.

Each filter removes a group that differs from the rest. Households without transport are less likely to reach an out-of-town centre; people who work weekends are elsewhere; people in a hurry, and those who dislike being approached, walk past. What remains is not a small copy of the town but a particular slice of it - on average more mobile, more likely to have weekend leisure, and more willing to engage with a seller.

The mechanism that makes this dangerous is that those same characteristics are related to spending. A slice of the population that is more mobile and has weekend time available is likely to report higher willingness to buy than the town as a whole, so the estimate is pulled upwards by the selection rather than by the demand. The arithmetic afterwards is faultless, which is what keeps the error out of sight.
marking_guidance: The mechanism must be traced step by step, because an asserted effect is not an explained one.

items.prompt: A retailer emails a satisfaction survey to 500 customers. Sixty reply, and 48 of those rate the service good or better. Analyse how acting on the resulting figure could damage the business.

The measurable consequence is that customer losses continue at the rate that prompted the survey, while the budget that could have addressed them is spent elsewhere.

items.prompt: A wholesaler is deciding whether to stock a new product on the strength of a market report published by the product's manufacturer. Evaluate whether it should.
items.canonical_answer:
It should treat the report as one input and not as the basis of the decision.

The decisive criterion is who had an interest in the result. The manufacturer gains from the wholesaler stocking the product, and it chose what to measure, whom to ask and what to publish. None of that makes the figures false, but it means the report is unlikely to contain the findings that would argue against stocking, and the wholesaler has no way of telling from the document what was left out. Where the method - sample size, selection, dates, response rate - is not published, the reliability of the figures cannot be judged at all.

The strongest argument the other way is that the manufacturer is often the only party that has researched this product, because nobody else had a reason to. Refusing to read it means deciding on less evidence rather than on better evidence, and a wholesaler that ignores every interested source ends up relying on its own records, which describe the products it already carries.

On balance the report should be used for what it can support - that the product exists, what it costs, what the manufacturer is claiming - and tested against something the manufacturer did not produce: the wholesaler's own sales of comparable lines, or a limited trial in two branches before a full order.

The judgement would shift if the report published its method and sample in full, or if the wholesaler could buy the product on sale-or-return, because the cost of being wrong would then be small enough that the weaker evidence would be enough to act on.

Mean = total of the values / number of values. The total is N$1 000, so the mean = 1 000 / 10 = N$100.

Median = the middle value once the values are in order. With ten values the two middle ones are the fifth and sixth, N$55 and N$60, so the median = (55 + 60) / 2 = N$57.50.

Nine of the ten customers spent less than the mean, which is pulled upwards by the single N$490 order. For a wholesaler asking what a typical customer spends, the median is the figure that answers the question.

If the real cause was portion size or waiting time, the price cut does not touch it. The measurable consequence is that takings fall further: the same reduced number of customers now pay less each, so revenue drops by more than the 14%, and margin drops with it.

items.prompt: Identify the order in which a table of market data should be read before any conclusion is drawn from it.
items.canonical_answer:
Begin with what the data is, not with the numbers.

First, read the title: what is being measured. Second, read the column headings and the units: tonnes or N$, thousands or millions, share or absolute amount. Third, read the period each column covers, and check that the columns cover equal periods. Fourth, read the source and the date of collection.

Only then carry out the reading itself: compare the rows, calculate the change between periods, and state what the numbers do.

What you finish with is a statement that can be defended - a change of a stated size, in a stated unit, over a stated period, from a named source. Taking the steps out of order is how a figure in units gets compared with a figure in value, or a quarter with a year.
marking_guidance: Steps: the order must be given as an order, not as a list of things to look at.
Input: the answer must start from what the table itself supplies - title, headings, units, period, source.
Each step must state what is read or calculated at that point.
Result: the answer must end with what the reader has at the end - a defensible statement with its unit and period.

items.prompt: Namib Tiles sold 80 000 tiles in 2023, when the whole market took 400 000 tiles, and 90 000 tiles in 2025, when the market took 500 000. Explain what happened to the business over those two years.
items.canonical_answer:
Compare the two rows on both measures, because they say different things.

In absolute terms the business grew: 10 000 more tiles, a rise of 10 000 / 80 000 = 0.125, or 12.5%. In share terms it shrank: 80 000 / 400 000 = 0.20 in 2023 against 90 000 / 500 000 = 0.18 in 2025, a fall of 2 percentage points.

Both are true, and the reason they point in different directions is that the market grew faster than Namib Tiles did - 100 000 / 400 000 = 0.25, a 25% rise against the firm's 12.5%. Of the 100 000 extra tiles sold in the market, rivals took 90 000.

What it means is that a good year in the sales ledger sits inside a weakening competitive position. The sales figure alone would have the business expanding; the share figure alone would have it in decline; read together, they say it expanded into a market that was expanding faster, and that is the finding a plan has to answer.
marking_guidance: Comparison: the sales figures must be compared against the market figures, not read on their own.
Meaning: the answer must say what the two readings together mean for the firm's competitive position.

items.prompt:
This table shows one year in a regional cement market, measured in tonnes.

| | Tonnes |
|---|---|
| Whole market | 840 000 |
| Producer A | 252 000 |
| Producer B | 168 000 |

Calculate the market share by volume held by Producer A, by Producer B, and by all other producers together.
items.canonical_answer:
Market share = the producer's sales / total market sales, here on volume.

Producer A: 252 000 / 840 000 = 0.30, a share of 30%.

Producer B: 168 000 / 840 000 = 0.20, a share of 20%.

Together A and B sell 252 000 + 168 000 = 420 000 tonnes, so the rest of the market sells 840 000 - 420 000 = 420 000 tonnes, which is 420 000 / 840 000 = 0.5, a share of 50%.

Half the market is therefore spread among producers other than the two largest, which tells a business entering this market that no single rival dominates it and that buyers here are used to dealing with smaller suppliers.
marking_guidance: Formula: market share = the producer's sales / total market sales, stated as a percentage and on a stated basis.
Substitution must be shown, not only the answer.
Units: every figure is in tonnes, and a share is expressed as a percentage, not as a tonnage.
Interpretation: one sentence saying what the spread of shares means for a business entering this market.

items.prompt: Correct this reading: 'Sales rose steeply this year - the plotted line climbs most of the height of the page.' The vertical axis of the drawing runs from 970 to 1 010 units, and monthly sales moved from 980 to 1 000.
items.canonical_answer:
The line is drawn correctly and the reading of it is wrong.

Sales moved 1 000 - 980 = 20 units, and 20 / 980 = 0.02, a rise of about 2%. The line looks steep because the vertical axis covers only 40 units, from 970 to 1 010, so 20 units of change fill half the picture. Drawn on an axis starting at zero, the same change would be a line that looks almost flat.

The correction is a habit rather than a calculation: read the axis, its starting value and its range, before reading the shape of the line. The same trap works in reverse - a tall axis can make a serious decline look like a gentle drift.
marking_guidance: The correction must identify the axis as the cause of the impression and quantify the actual change.

items.prompt: A lodge's bookings and its advertising spending both rose through the year. Explain why that pattern on its own does not show that the advertising caused the bookings.
items.canonical_answer:
Two series moving together is a statement about the shape of two lines, and three different situations produce the same shape.

The advertising may have brought the bookings, which is the reading the lodge would like. Or the influence may run the other way: a lodge that sees bookings filling has more cash and more confidence, so it spends more on advertising - the bookings caused the spending. Or both may be following something neither line shows, such as a rise in tourist arrivals to the region, which fills the lodge and prompts every operator in the area to advertise at the same time.

Nothing in the pattern separates those three, because all three produce two rising lines. Separating them needs evidence the pattern cannot supply: a period in which one moved and the other did not, regional arrivals data showing whether the whole area filled, or a deliberate test - holding advertising flat for a month in a comparable season and watching what bookings do.
marking_guidance: The mechanism must be traced step by step, because an asserted effect is not an explained one.

items.prompt: A manager reports: 'Our share of the market is up from 9% to 11%, so the new packaging worked.' The table the figures come from also shows total market volume falling from 2.4 million units to 1.8 million. Explain what the manager has missed.
items.canonical_answer:
Read the share against the market volume it is a share of, because the second column changes what the first one means.

In the first year the business sold 0.09 x 2 400 000 = 216 000 units. In the second it sold 0.11 x 1 800 000 = 198 000 units. Its share rose two percentage points and its sales fell by 18 000 units, because the market shrank faster than the business did.

The second thing missed is the attribution. Even on the rising share, the table shows two things moving together - new packaging and a higher share - and that is an association rather than proof of a cause. A shrinking market in which weaker rivals leave first raises the share of everyone who stays, packaging or no packaging.

The conclusion the manager should have reached is that the business is holding up better than its market, which is worth knowing, and that it is selling less than it was; and that testing the packaging needs evidence the table cannot supply, such as sales in comparable areas where the packaging was not changed.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use both columns of the manager's own table - the share and the market volume.
Reasoning: the reasoning must convert the shares into units before drawing any conclusion.
Conclusion: the answer must conclude what the manager can and cannot claim.

items.prompt: Oshikango Uniforms is about to start making school uniforms. Its owner has written two lines about the market: 'parents buy school uniforms' and 'there are plenty of schools here'. Identify what a usable description of this market and its buyers would add to those two lines, and explain what each addition would let the owner settle.
items.canonical_answer:
The size of the market, in both measures. How many uniforms are bought in the town in a year, and what they sell for. Volume tells the owner how many machines and how much fabric are needed; value tells her what revenue is available to be won. 'Plenty of schools' supports neither figure.

The growth of the market. Whether the number of learners is rising, flat or falling decides whether the business is entering something expanding or competing for a fixed quantity of work.

Who already supplies it, and how the share is divided. If two tailors already hold contracts with most schools, the work has to be taken from them, and the owner needs a reason parents or schools would move - price, fit, delivery date.

The difference between the customer and the consumer. The parent buys and the learner wears. The parent's questions are price and durability; the learner's are fit and comfort, and it is the learner's experience that decides whether the same supplier is used next year.

A profile made of things the owner can act on. Where these parents shop, when in the year they buy, what they spend per child, how they pay. Each of those settles a decision she has to take anyway - where to sell from, when to hold stock, what price points to cut for, and what the till has to accept. A profile recording that parents want good uniforms at fair prices is true and settles nothing.
marking_guidance: Each point must be stated plainly before it is explained.
The reason each addition matters must be given - what the owner could decide with it that she cannot decide now.
The context must be used: these are additions to this owner's two lines, about a uniform business in a specific town, and each must attach to a decision she faces.
A multi-part practice task: it asks for several additions, so it carries no single paper tariff.

items.prompt:
Kavango Solar installs household solar kits in Rundu. It surveyed 250 households out of the 9 000 in its service area, approaching people at a shopping centre on two Saturday mornings; a further 40 of those approached declined to answer. The results were:

| Price of kit | Households saying they would buy |
|---|---|
| N$6 000 | 145 |
| N$7 500 | 90 |
| N$9 000 | 40 |

Calculate the percentage saying they would buy at each price and what the N$7 500 figure implies for the service area; taking the margin of error as about 1 divided by the square root of the sample size, calculate the range around that figure; and evaluate whether Kavango Solar should set its price at N$7 500 on this evidence.
items.canonical_answer:
Percentages: 145 / 250 = 0.58, so 58% at N$6 000; 90 / 250 = 0.36, so 36% at N$7 500; 40 / 250 = 0.16, so 16% at N$9 000.

Scaled to the service area at N$7 500: 0.36 x 9 000 = 3 240 households.

Margin of error: the square root of 250 is about 15.8, and 1 / 15.8 = 0.063, so about 6 percentage points either way. The true proportion is likely to lie between 30% and 42%, which is between 0.30 x 9 000 = 2 700 and 0.42 x 9 000 = 3 780 households. At N$7 500 a kit that is revenue somewhere between 2 700 x 7 500 = N$20 250 000 and 3 780 x 7 500 = N$28 350 000.

Judgement: Kavango Solar should not fix the price at N$7 500 on this evidence, though it should keep the price in the range the survey points at while it gets better evidence.

The decisive criterion is the reliability of the sample measured against the size of what is being committed. Everyone in the sample was at one shopping centre, on a weekend morning, and willing to stop: households without transport and people working weekends are under-represented, and 250 / 290 = 0.862, so 14% of those approached declined and cannot be assumed to resemble those who answered. On top of that, a solar kit at N$7 500 is a large outlay for a household, and a stated intention that costs nothing to give tends to run ahead of a purchase that has to be paid for. Every one of those points pushes the 36% the same way, which is upwards.

The strongest argument the other way is that the shape of the responses is informative even if the level is not. Demand falls from 58% to 36% to 16% across two price steps, and a bias that makes people readier to say yes does not obviously change which price they say yes at. That pattern is worth something: it puts the usable price range below N$9 000, where fewer than one household in six stayed interested.

The condition that would settle it is evidence of purchase rather than intention: install at N$7 500 in one district for a month and count orders, which costs far less than a mispriced launch across the service area. Interviews with the households that refused at N$9 000 would add the reason behind the number - whether the obstacle is the price itself or the payment terms - and a monthly payment option may matter more here than the headline figure.
marking_guidance: All the stated figures must be calculated with working shown.
Judgement: the answer must recommend a course of action, not set out both cases and stop.
Context: the recommendation must rest on how Kavango Solar's own sample was drawn, not on sampling in the abstract.
Criterion: the decisive factor is the reliability of the sample weighed against the size of the commitment.
Counterargument: must credit what the response pattern across the three prices does establish.
Condition: must name the evidence that would settle it, and say what qualitative work would add.

context.situation: setting a launch price from a shopping-centre survey

items.prompt: Oshakati Poultry is deciding whether to launch packaged chicken portions. It has N$45 000 for research and eight weeks before the packaging order must be placed. A published report on Namibian meat consumption costs N$5 000, covers the last six years and rests on fieldwork carried out in 2024. A research firm quotes N$38 000 for 400 in-store interviews and a two-week sales test in one branch, and needs six weeks to deliver. Analyse the circumstances under which each of these is the better use of the budget, and evaluate what Oshakati Poultry should do.
items.canonical_answer:
The report is the better use of the money where the question still open is whether the market is large enough and moving the right way. It covers six years, so it shows the direction of meat consumption nationally, and at N$5 000 it costs about an eighth of the fieldwork. If it showed consumption of the relevant kind flat or falling, the decision would be settled for N$5 000 and the remaining N$40 000 would never need to be spent.

The fieldwork is the better use where the question is one no existing source can contain. Packaged portions from this producer do not yet exist, so nobody has collected data on whether Oshakati shoppers would buy them or at what price. The two-week sales test is the stronger half of that quote, because it records purchases rather than intentions, and the 400 interviews can reach the shoppers in this town rather than a national average that blends them with Windhoek.

The circumstances that would make the fieldwork the wrong choice are time and commitment size. It needs six of the eight weeks available, leaving two weeks to analyse and act, and N$38 000 is a large sum for a business of this size to commit before knowing whether the market is there at all.

Recommendation: buy the report first, and commission the fieldwork only if the report supports going on. The decisive factor is the order of the two questions - the size question is answerable cheaply from data that already exists, and the price and willingness question is not answerable from it at all. Reversing the order risks spending N$38 000 to price a product for a market the report could have shown was shrinking.

The strongest argument against sequencing is the calendar: the report has to be read and the fieldwork commissioned inside the first two weeks, or the six weeks it needs will not fit before the packaging order. That is manageable but tight, and it is the condition on which the recommendation depends. If the report cannot be obtained and read within about ten days, the better course is to commission a narrower and faster piece of fieldwork - the two-week sales test alone - and drop the interviews, because a test that records actual purchases answers the decisive question with less of the budget and less of the calendar.
marking_guidance: Both sets of circumstances must be analysed before a recommendation is reached.
Judgement: a recommendation is required.
Context: the answer must use Oshakati Poultry's own facts - the N$45 000, the eight weeks, the two quoted options.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be which question each source can answer, and in what order.
Counterargument: must address the calendar risk that sequencing creates.
Condition: must state what would change the recommendation.

context.situation: choosing between a published report and commissioned fieldwork before a launch
facts: eight weeks to the packaging order
fieldwork quote N$38 000, six weeks, 400 interviews and a two-week sales test

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: A furniture retailer in Windhoek is deciding whether to open a second branch in Otjiwarongo. Its owner proposes to decide entirely on published data - national household spending figures from 2023, the town's population from the last census, and a competitor's annual report. Evaluate whether that is a sound basis for the decision.
items.canonical_answer:
Judgement to reach: the published data is a sound basis for deciding whether to look further, and not a sound basis for committing to a branch.

Paragraph 1 - what these sources can support. They are cheap, quick and already cover the whole country and a run of years. Population and national spending together give an order of magnitude for furniture spending in the town, which is enough to rule the idea out if the number is small.

Paragraph 2 - the reliability question applied to each source in turn. The spending figures are from 2023 and the decision is about the years ahead, so the older they are and the faster incomes have moved, the less they describe the present. The census figure ages the same way and counts residents rather than buyers. The competitor's annual report was written to be read by shareholders, its author had an interest in how the business looks, and its method for any market figure it quotes is not disclosed.

Paragraph 3 - the mechanism by which this goes wrong. National averages blend Otjiwarongo with Windhoek, where incomes and furniture spending differ; the owner sizes the branch on a national average, signs a lease for that size, and carries the fixed cost of a shop the local market cannot fill.

Paragraph 4 - the strongest case for the owner's position. The cost of the published route is a few thousand rand against tens of thousands for fieldwork, and the first question - is there any plausible market here at all - genuinely is answerable from it. Refusing to start with secondary data would be spending the fieldwork budget to learn what is already written down.

Judgement and condition: use the published data to screen the idea, then spend a small amount on primary work aimed only at what it cannot answer - what Otjiwarongo households currently buy furniture for, where they buy it now, and whether they would travel less far to buy it. The condition on which the whole recommendation rests is the size of the commitment: a short lease on a small shop is a different risk from a five-year lease, and the larger the irreversible commitment, the weaker the case for deciding on published data alone.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay - structure with a stated judgement is what is assessed.
Judgement: the plan must show where the recommendation is reached.
Context: the plan must handle the three named sources and the Otjiwarongo decision, not secondary data in general.
Criterion: the decisive factor must be which questions published data can and cannot answer, judged by how it was produced.
Counterargument: must include the genuine case for starting with the published sources.
Condition: must end on what would change the answer - the size and reversibility of the commitment.

context.situation: deciding on a second branch from published data alone
